name: Karl Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the trumpet section in a civic orchestra, record practice entries and coach four young brass players. I have a master's degree in music and have led sections for thirty-one years; conductors trust me with a difficult opening. The sound I love is four brass players landing a soft note together.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58, my partner works changing hours in a school cafeteria, and our children are grown. The orchestra's community contract pays below what a lead player normally earns, and there are few similar posts nearby. We rent and have three weeks of expenses saved after replacing a broken heating system. I use AI daily to draft rehearsal maps and check my own part, but I play every line before sharing it.

I'd say **four trumpets** still need a live first breath.
think: Our **three-week reserve** and changing partner hours make cancellations hard.
The **low community fee** remains a problem even if AI is mild.
do: Confirm **four paid calls** and four pupils; request written cancellation pay.
Check **existing AI maps** against the conductor’s marked score before sharing.
Save **one fifth** of extra cleared concert pay after rent, food and horn repairs toward one rehearsal fee.
feel: I feel **anxious** about ordinary gaps in orchestra pay.
S0.quote: A missed entrance can ruin the whole brass chord.
fieldNote: His **senior trumpet skill** coexists with low community-contract pay and three weeks saved.
Daily **AI rehearsal maps** are existing use, manually checked against the score and played aloud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the orchestra a quicker rehearsal map is fine if paid preparation stays beside the date. Four trumpets still need a person to give the first breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three weeks saved and my partner's changing cafeteria shifts make a moved concert hard already. Mild AI doesn't change the community contract's low fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll confirm four paid orchestra calls and my four pupils, and ask the manager for a written cancellation fee. In the first year of this mild change I'll keep checking daily AI maps against the conductor's marked score, and save one fifth of an extra cleared concert fee toward one rehearsal fee only after rent, food and horn repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about our ordinary pay gaps. Faster maps are pleasant, but the rent comes on its own date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when the concert moved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A concert moved last winter and the orchestra paid only the rehearsal. We used most of our reserve for rent before the next fee cleared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you check an AI rehearsal map?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't send an AI map without playing the line and checking the conductor's score. A missed entrance can ruin the whole brass chord.

say: I'd ask which **paid practice hours** software would remove.
I'd demand **separate written fees** for leading and preparation.
think: Entries and maps bring **one-third** of my own pay.
Our **three-week reserve** cannot cover a long senior-job search.
do: Request **paid checker demo** outside booked calls; test only owned nameless part with funded paid-use licence and approved local storage.
Play **each changed bar** against paper; stop wrong notes/leaks and require written learner permission before other audio.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a realistic cut to preparation income.
S1.quote: I can learn a tool quickly, but a neat file is not an orchestra wage.
fieldNote: His **new AI trial** needs paid instruction, owned nameless music, permitted paid use and approved local storage.
He **checks bars manually** and stops for wrong notes or data leaving the orchestra.

steps.text: Count ten paid entry invoices this month
Take paid checker demo outside calls; test owned nameless part with funded paid-use licence/local storage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the orchestra which paid practice-entry and rehearsal-map hours its software would remove. I'd ask the board to price my live section-leading and preparation separately before rewriting the contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Practice entries and maps bring about a third of my own pay. If the board buys fewer, our three-week reserve and thin local list of senior jobs make the gap immediate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll count ten entry invoices and bring the numbers to the board, then ask for a paid demonstration of a new AI part checker on a nameless trumpet part I own. In the first year I'll test it only if the orchestra funds a licence permitting paid use and approved local storage, outside paid calls; I'll play every changed bar against paper and stop wrong notes or a file leaving the orchestra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a realistic cut to my own paid preparation. I can learn a tool quickly, but a neat file is not an orchestra wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you test on a pupil's music?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, a pupil's part would stay out of my trial. Any learner recording would need written permission and a clear storage rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who pays for the demonstration?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The orchestra must pay the instructor without replacing a booked call. If it wants me to buy the trial, I'll use my pencil marks.

I'd seek **signed live section calls** now.
think: I expect **one-third pay** from entries and maps to end in 2028.
Further **live performance cuts** remain possible, not my forecast.
do: Total **entry/map fees**, seek signed orchestra calls and request actual pension statements before stopping work.
Seek **posted brass coach** after live cuts if master’s/leadership qualify; require paid human coaching, written replacement net after travel and buses.
Keep **orchestra and pupils** until a suitable signed offer.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about expected pay loss against three weeks saved.
S2.quote: A master's degree will not tell me what retirement pays each month.
fieldNote: Expected **2028 entry/map loss** precedes 2031 playing robots; live cuts remain conditional.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the brass section that thinking AGI by 2028 could make practice entries before a robot plays trumpet. Trumpet-playing robots follow around 2031, so I want signed live section calls now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the orchestra to stop buying entries and maps in 2028, taking about a third of my pay. Live performances might also fall, but the current calls are still signed. I wake at night counting the paid calls that would be left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll total entry and map fees, seek signed paid orchestra calls and request actual pension statements before considering a stop at 60. In the first year after 2028, if paid live calls also fall, I'll seek a posted paid brass-coach role only if the employer accepts my master's degree and section-leading experience, real live coaching hours are paid, and written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and buses fit the hours; I'll keep orchestra and pupils until a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about the expected third of my pay disappearing with three weeks saved. A live-call collapse would be worse, but I won't call it certain because of an AI card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a brass-coach post open now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No music centre has offered me a brass-coach role. I would read a current paid posting and hours before treating it as an option.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you know your pension amount?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have not received a pension statement. A master's degree will not tell me what retirement pays each month.

say: I'd price a **paid brass clinic** during the warning years.
I'd sign **room and insurance costs** before taking deposits.
think: Ordinary software may cut **paid maps before 2031**.
Our **thin reserve** cannot pay hall hire for an empty class.
do: Offer **brass clinic** after written room/insurance charges; eight fees cover room, insurance, cleaning/mouthpieces, own teaching/prep, paid pianist and travel outside calls.
Inspect **eight loan horns** or sound own instruments; defer/refund everyone below eight safe paid places.
Renew **after 2031** only with eight safe fees covering room/insurance/cleaning/mouthpieces/teaching/preparation/pianist/travel and written terms; keep paid orchestra/pupils.
feel: I feel **anxious** until fees cover both musicians and the hall.
S3.quote: A packed brass clinic can still lose money if its pianist and my preparation are unpaid.
fieldNote: His **senior mastery** supports the clinic, but the paid pianist and full own work must be covered.
The **eight-place floor** includes safe horns, room and insurance; every deposit is refunded below the floor.

steps.text: Start clinic after written room/insurance; eight fees cover room, insurance, cleaning/mouthpieces, teaching/prep, pianist, travel
Inspect eight horns or sound own instruments; defer/refund whole group below eight safe paid places
Renew after 2031 with eight safe fees covering room/insurance/cleaning/mouthpieces/teaching/preparation/pianist/travel under written terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the town hall that five years to AGI by 2031 lets me price a live brass-section clinic, a short paid class, before the software replaces more entries. Playing robots follow around 2034; I would sign room and insurance costs before taking deposits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordinary software may cut paid maps before 2031. I can teach a section to breathe together, but I can't turn three weeks of savings into room hire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next autumn I'll get written room hire, charges and insurance terms before deposits for a separate four-week brass clinic outside booked orchestra and pupil hours. Eight adults must prepay enough for room, insurance, cleaning and safe mouthpieces, my teaching and preparation, a paid pianist for accompaniments, and travel; the hall lends eight horns and its keeper inspects them without charge, or players bring sound instruments. In the first year after 2031 I'll renew only with the same full-cost eight safe paid places and written terms; if fewer pay or a horn fails without replacement, I'll defer and refund the whole group while keeping paid orchestra work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious until eight fees cover both musicians and the hall. A packed brass clinic can still lose money if its pianist and my preparation are unpaid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a loan horn fails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A loose slide or a dirty mouthpiece makes a place unsafe. If there aren't eight sound instruments, I refund all deposits instead of borrowing from our rent account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the clinic replace paid orchestra time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the clinic is on a free afternoon. I won't swap a signed orchestra call or pupil lesson for eight names without fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grown children that ten years to AGI by 2036 lets us get actual pension figures and paid orchestra calls on paper. Trumpet-playing robots follow around 2039, but our rent arrives before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may still need paid leading and teaching. Three weeks saved now and an unknown pension are no retirement plan, however long the warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll request actual pension statements and a written two-year paid section-call plan, then save ten percent of each extra cleared festival performance fee after rent, food and horn repairs toward two months of expenses. In the first year after 2036 I'll keep paid orchestra and pupil work while booked; I'll renew the separate brass clinic only outside paid calls after written room-hire charges and insurance are confirmed before deposits, with eight safe prepaid places covering room, insurance, cleaning, mouthpieces, my teaching/preparation, paid pianist and travel under written terms, otherwise deferring and refunding the whole group. I'll slow paid work only if verified pension payments and booked fees cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about reaching 68 with only three weeks saved now. Ten years lets me check actual pension figures; it does not make an unpaid rehearsal pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no extra festival pays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If no extra festival performance pays, nothing from it goes into savings. I won't move rent money to make the target look met.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you seen pension figures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we have not received pension figures yet. I will read the statements before giving up a booked orchestra call.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because entry and map fees could end before another paid senior role appears. Signed orchestra calls, actual pension figures and a posted qualifying brass-coach job with written net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the accompanist when a brass class fills. Eight names on a brass-clinic list are not eight safe paid places.

headlineQuote: Eight names on a brass-clinic list are not eight safe paid places.
portrait: Karl is a **58-year-old trumpet section lead** with a music master's degree, partner and grown children.
His **low pay**, three-week reserve and few nearby senior jobs persist despite excellent playing skill.
He uses **AI daily** for rehearsal maps, learning a new checker only through paid, private and manually checked trials.
He tests a **separate brass clinic** only with eight safe full-cost fees, a paid pianist and no displaced paid work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase a third of Karl's pay from entries and maps.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed orchestra calls**, actual pension figures and posted qualifying coaching with written after-travel replacement pay would help.
